title: Spring top sellers and the stores

brief.decision: Which products get an in-store display next spring
brief.deadline: The display planning meeting at the end of the month

checkpoints.prompt: Write the query that answers Fleur's question.

Fleur's headline: of all the units Voltmarkt sold from 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31, both days included, what percentage were sold on lines whose channel is 'store'? Use every line of the sales table with an order_date in that period, whatever the product; a line with a missing units value adds nothing. Divide the store units by all the units and multiply by 100. Type the percentage with 1 decimal, for example 12.5.

model_plan:
Metric formula: units is the sum of units; store_units is the sum of units over the lines whose channel is 'store', 0 when there are none.
Output grain: one row per product, cut to the 10 with the most units.
Tables and keys: the sales view only, one row per order line; group on product_id and product_name.
Filters: order_date from 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31, both days included.
Edge cases: a missing units value adds nothing, a product with no store lines needs 0 rather than a missing value, and equal units are settled by product_id before the cut.
Expected row count: 10
model_answer_template: In the first quarter of 2025, {CP4} percent of all the units Voltmarkt sold went through the stores, so in-store displays can reach most of the volume. A ranking by units favours small, fast-moving items, and these may bring in little money per unit, so look at what the top 10 holds. Units say nothing about margin or about whether a display adds sales, and one quarter may not repeat next spring. Next, rank the same products by net revenue and margin, and try the displays in a few stores before rolling them out.
follow_up_question: How do the same products rank by net revenue instead of units?
